Chapter 9: Motherhood—Between Sacrifice and Selfhood.
When people talk about motherhood, they often call it the most natural thing in the world. Some say it's a calling, or even a destiny—a source of endless joy. But if you ask most mothers, they’ll tell you the truth is a whole lot messier.
The choice to become a mother—or not—isn’t just personal. It’s tangled up in expectations, pressures, and your own hopes for the future.
Picture this: a woman holds her newborn for the very first time. The room is still, and everything feels new. Sure, there’s a rush of love, but there’s also fear. She wonders, "Am I enough? Will I lose myself? Can I measure up to this idea of the perfect mother?"
From day one, advice and opinions come pouring in—some helpful, some not so much, and most of it pointing in different directions. Be nurturing, but don’t smother. Put your kids first, but remember your needs. Work hard, but never let your job come before your family. It’s a lot to juggle.
Most people don’t realize just how heavy these expectations can be. Mothers are told to sacrifice—time, energy, even dreams they once had. There’s this belief that a good mom always puts her children first, no matter what.
And then there’s the balancing act—work, family, ambition—and the guilt that sneaks in, no matter which path you take. Give up your career? Some will judge. Go after your goals? Others will criticize.
The world is quick to judge, but slow to offer real support. Childcare costs a fortune, most workplaces aren’t exactly flexible, and not every partner pulls their weight. If a mother asks for help, she might be seen as weak. If she tries to do it all, people might applaud—but often, it comes at a huge personal price.
But here’s something remarkable: within all those challenges, there’s room for growth. Some women find strengths they never knew they had. They learn to set boundaries, ask for the help they deserve, and make space for themselves. There’s joy in the little things—a child’s giggle, a quiet evening, a moment of real connection that says more than words ever could.
Motherhood isn’t destiny—it’s just one path out of many. Every woman needs to find her own way. Some decide not to have children, and that comes with its own questions and judgments. Others become mothers in ways that don’t fit the usual mold—through adoption, blended families, or shared parenting. And all these choices are valid.
The real truth? There’s no one way to be a mother—or to feel fulfilled. When women make their own choices about family, work, and who they want to be, they take better care of themselves and the people they love. And by doing that, they push back against a world that too often tries to measure them by what they give, instead of who they truly are.
